reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Defined by a persistent or recurrent ear discharge through a chronic tympanic membrane perforation with associated hearing loss
Traditionally divided into a tubotympanic (mucosal, safe) type and an atticoantral (squamous, unsafe) type associated with cholesteatoma
The tubotympanic type typically causes intermittent painless mucoid discharge and a central perforation, with a comparatively low complication risk
The atticoantral type is dangerous because cholesteatoma erodes bone and predisposes to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications
Foul-smelling scanty discharge, an attic or marginal perforation, or visible keratin debris should raise suspicion of cholesteatoma
Management principles include aural toileting, topical and systemic antibiotics for active disease, and surgery to eradicate disease and reconstruct hearing
Cholesteatoma is essentially a surgical disease requiring mastoid exploration to remove the sac and prevent complications
Audiometry usually shows conductive loss, but a sensorineural component suggests inner ear involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic suppurative otitis media is long-standing inflammation of the middle ear cleft with a non-intact tympanic membrane. In the tubotympanic type, persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent infection maintain mucosal inflammation and a central perforation, with reversible mucosal changes. In the atticoantral type, retraction pockets or migration of squamous epithelium form a cholesteatoma, an expanding keratinising sac whose enzymatic and pressure effects erode ossicles and surrounding bone. This bony destruction can breach the facial canal, labyrinth, or dural plates, opening routes for intracranial spread.
additionalDifferentials: Middle ear or external canal malignancy
Retained foreign body with secondary infection
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and otomicroscopy to define perforation type and detect cholesteatoma
Pure tone audiometry to characterise conductive or mixed hearing loss
Culture and sensitivity of ear discharge
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to map cholesteatoma extent and bony erosion
MRI where intracranial complications or residual cholesteatoma are suspected
redFlags: Foul discharge with an attic or marginal perforation suggesting cholesteatoma
Vertigo or a positive fistula sign indicating labyrinthine erosion
Facial nerve palsy from facial canal involvement
Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial extension
reference.prognosis: The mucosal (tubotympanic) type generally does well with medical treatment and reconstructive surgery, while the atticoantral type with cholesteatoma carries a higher risk of serious complications and requires surgical eradication with ongoing follow-up for recurrence.
pitfalls: Treating a discharging ear as simple otitis externa and missing an underlying cholesteatoma
Failing to recognise attic or marginal perforations as high-risk
Overlooking early complications such as vertigo or facial weakness
Relying on medical therapy alone when surgical clearance of cholesteatoma is required
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Regular aural toileting by microsuction to clear discharge and debris from the middle ear
Topical antibiotic ear drops such as a quinolone (ciprofloxacin) for active mucosal disease, preferring non-ototoxic agents
Culture-guided systemic antibiotics, including antipseudomonal cover, for extensive or complicated infection
Surgical eradication of cholesteatoma by mastoidectomy in atticoantral (unsafe) disease to prevent intratemporal and intracranial complications
Tympanoplasty with ossiculoplasty to repair the perforation and reconstruct hearing
Water precautions to keep the ear dry, with hearing rehabilitation including hearing aids where needed
ENT follow-up with surveillance for recurrence, residual cholesteatoma and complications
